title: Week 34 · Lesson 58: HIV, PrEP & STI Pharmacology — Prevention, Treatment, Interactions & FNP Care
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 34 — Lesson 58: HIV, PrEP & STI Pharmacology — Prevention, Treatment, Interactions & FNP Care

FNP-level goal: Deliver stigma-free, confidential, evidence-based HIV and STI care by distinguishing urgent PEP from ongoing PrEP and HIV treatment; using accurate testing, interaction review, reproductive counseling, partner services, and timely specialty/public-health coordination.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate HIV treatment, PrEP, PEP, and STI treatment/prevention goals.
  • Explain why HIV status must be confirmed before initiating PrEP and why potential PEP exposures require time-sensitive assessment.
  • Recognize antiretroviral interaction principles and the importance of complete medication reconciliation.
  • Apply a patient-centered approach to sexual history, testing, adherence, confidentiality, partner services, and stigma.
  • Identify acute HIV, STI, medication-toxicity, pregnancy, assault, and post-exposure situations requiring urgent escalation or consultation.

Part 1 — Sexual Health Is Routine Primary Care

HIV and STI care belongs in routine FNP practice. Asking about sexual health, gender identity, anatomy relevant to care, partners, practices, pregnancy intention, contraception, substance use, injection equipment, prior STI history, and prevention goals allows the clinician to offer testing and prevention without making assumptions about identity or behavior.

Use neutral, normalized language: “I ask all my patients these questions because sexual health is part of health.” A respectful history is not a risk score performed on a patient; it is the beginning of individualized prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and support.

Part 2 — Four Different Medication Goals

Antiretroviral therapy (ART) treats HIV in a person with confirmed infection. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) uses antiretroviral medication to prevent HIV in people without HIV who may be exposed. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is a time-sensitive emergency intervention after a possible exposure in a person without HIV. STI treatment treats a diagnosed or suspected infection and often includes prevention of reinfection and partner-management steps.

These goals should never be blended. Giving partial antiretroviral therapy to a person with unrecognized HIV can create safety and resistance concerns. Giving PEP too late misses a time-sensitive opportunity. Treating a patient’s STI while ignoring partners, prevention, and retesting can lead to reinfection and ongoing transmission.

Part 3 — HIV Testing Is Clinical Decision Support

HIV testing supports diagnosis, treatment, PrEP eligibility, PEP assessment, and prevention planning. The correct test strategy depends on symptoms, timing of possible exposure, prior or recent antiretroviral use, and the clinical question. Acute HIV can present with nonspecific fever, rash, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, fatigue, myalgias, headache, or gastrointestinal symptoms—or with no distinctive symptoms at all.

Do not treat one negative test as a universal answer without considering the exposure timeline and test window. Use the current CDC testing algorithm and seek expert support when recent PrEP/PEP use, symptoms of acute HIV, or discordant results complicate interpretation.

Part 4 — PEP Is a Time-Sensitive Emergency

PEP is considered after a potential HIV exposure through sexual contact, shared injection equipment, or relevant mucous-membrane, nonintact-skin, or percutaneous exposure. HIV can establish infection quickly; CDC recommends rapid evaluation when a patient presents within 72 hours of a potential exposure. Do not delay indicated PEP solely because every baseline result, source detail, or specialist callback is not yet available.

Assess exposure type, timing, source information when available, patient HIV status, current/recent PrEP or PEP use, pregnancy possibility, kidney disease, medications, hepatitis status, and assault-related needs. If PEP is indicated, follow current emergency protocol and arrange prompt follow-up. Exposures beyond the PEP window still deserve HIV/STI testing, counseling, and prevention planning.

Part 5 — PrEP Is Ongoing Prevention Care

PrEP is for people without HIV who may be exposed through sex or injection drug use. It should be offered without stigma, including to anyone who requests it. Before initiation, clinicians must confirm that the patient does not have HIV and complete the current baseline assessment required for the chosen medication and delivery method.

PrEP is more than a prescription. It includes adherence or appointment support, HIV testing, kidney-function or other medication-specific monitoring, STI testing, pregnancy/reproductive counseling, vaccination and prevention review, mental-health and substance-use support when wanted, and a plan for missed doses or discontinued medication. Use the current CDC guidance because available options and follow-up requirements change.

Part 6 — ART Is Lifelong, Individualized Treatment

For a person with HIV, ART aims to suppress viral replication, preserve immune function, improve health, and prevent transmission. Regimen selection depends on treatment history, resistance information, comorbidities, hepatitis status, kidney/liver function, pregnancy considerations, concurrent medications, accessibility, and patient preferences.

Do not advise a patient with HIV to stop, split, or substitute ART because of a routine side effect or an unrelated acute illness without prompt HIV-care consultation. Abrupt interruption can have serious consequences. The FNP role includes adherence support, toxicity recognition, treatment of general medical conditions with interaction review, and expedited linkage to HIV specialty care when needed.

Part 7 — Antiretroviral Drug Interactions Are Common

Antiretroviral medications can have clinically significant interactions with commonly used therapies. Interactions can occur through absorption, metabolism, transport, or overlapping organ toxicity. Acid-reducing medications may affect absorption of selected antiretrovirals, while antacids or mineral supplements containing polyvalent cations can reduce absorption of some integrase inhibitors. Other medicines can change metabolic pathways and alter exposure.

Before adding, stopping, or changing any significant medication, review the exact ART or PrEP/PEP regimen using a current interaction resource. Include antacids, calcium/iron/magnesium products, vitamins, supplements, hormone therapy, statins, anticonvulsants, antimicrobials, psychiatric medicines, acid suppression, and recreational substances when clinically relevant.

Part 8 — Adherence Is a Systems Question

Medication adherence can be affected by stigma, cost, food insecurity, housing, transportation, immigration concerns, depression, trauma, cognitive burden, side effects, complex schedules, pharmacy access, and fear of disclosure. Avoid asking “Why are you noncompliant?” Instead ask, “How has taking this medicine been going?” and “What gets in the way on a difficult day?”

A practical plan may include simplified routines, reminders, discreet packaging, mail pharmacy, refill synchronization, insurance navigation, mental-health support, peer support, family support only with permission, or a different treatment approach. The goal is durable access and partnership, not blame.

Part 9 — STI Testing, Treatment, and Partner Services

STI symptoms may be absent, and the appropriate test can depend on the patient’s anatomy, sites of exposure, symptoms, pregnancy status, epidemiology, and sexual practices. Obtain specimens from clinically relevant sites, use current CDC testing and treatment guidance, and explain when results will return and what the patient should do while awaiting them.

Do not treat an STI result as the end of care. Discuss medication adherence, partner notification and treatment, prevention, and retesting when indicated. Options may include patient notification, public-health-assisted services, direct evaluation, and expedited partner therapy where allowed and clinically appropriate. Legal requirements and EPT availability vary by jurisdiction.

Part 10 — Pregnancy, Harm Reduction, and Whole-Person Care

Pregnancy intention and pregnancy status matter for HIV treatment, PrEP/PEP, STI testing, medication choice, and urgency of linkage to care. Do not use pregnancy as a reason to delay time-sensitive PEP evaluation, and do not advise a pregnant patient with HIV to stop ART abruptly. Coordinate promptly with experienced HIV and obstetric clinicians.

People who inject drugs may benefit from HIV testing, PrEP, hepatitis testing and vaccination as appropriate, sterile-equipment access, overdose prevention, and substance-use treatment when desired. Harm reduction lowers infection and overdose risk while preserving dignity and engagement.

Part 11 — Urgent Presentations and Confidentiality

Urgent or emergency assessment may be needed for a potential PEP exposure within the time window, sexual assault, severe medication reaction, anaphylaxis, acute neurologic symptoms, severe dehydration, altered mental status, suspected disseminated infection, severe pelvic or testicular pain, pregnancy with concerning infection symptoms, or a patient who is clinically unstable.

HIV and STI information is sensitive. Discuss preferred contact method, safe voicemail/text practices, patient portal privacy, pharmacy communication, and who may receive information. Follow applicable privacy laws and local public-health requirements. Never disclose a patient’s HIV or STI status without appropriate authorization or legal basis.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: An Exposure Last Night

A patient presents 18 hours after a possible sexual exposure to HIV and is visibly anxious. They have no current symptoms and ask whether they should wait for the source person’s test result.

FNP reasoning: time matters. Rapidly assess exposure, patient HIV status, current/recent PrEP or PEP use, pregnancy possibility, medications, and baseline tests according to current protocol. Do not delay indicated PEP solely to obtain every piece of information. Arrange follow-up and transition to ongoing prevention discussion when appropriate.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: PrEP Request Without Disclosed Risk

A patient requests PrEP but says they do not want to discuss detailed sexual history. They are worried they will be judged.

FNP reasoning: thank the patient for asking, explain that PrEP can be prescribed to people without HIV who request it, and invite—not force—discussion needed for safe medication selection and screening. Confirm HIV-negative status, complete current baseline assessment, offer confidential follow-up, and avoid gatekeeping based on disclosure comfort.

Part 14 — Clinical Case: New Antacid in a Patient on ART

A patient with well-controlled HIV starts an over-the-counter antacid and mineral supplement for reflux and fatigue. Several weeks later, they ask whether the products could affect their ART.

FNP reasoning: do not guess. Identify the exact ART regimen, products, timing, doses, kidney function, and other medicines. Use a current ARV interaction resource and coordinate with HIV pharmacy or the HIV-care team. Common nonprescription products can meaningfully affect absorption of selected regimens.

FNP HIV/STI Pharmacology Framework

  1. Normalize and ask: use a confidential, patient-centered sexual and exposure history.
  2. Define the goal: HIV diagnosis/ART, PrEP, time-sensitive PEP, STI testing/treatment, or prevention follow-up.
  3. Test correctly: choose current, timeline-aware HIV/STI testing and do not overinterpret one result.
  4. Reconcile: review all prescribed, nonprescription, supplement, and substance exposures for interactions.
  5. Coordinate: link HIV care, obstetric care, infectious-disease expertise, public health, pharmacy, and behavioral supports as needed.
  6. Protect dignity: use trauma-informed, stigma-free communication and accurate confidentiality counseling.

High-Yield Summary

ART: treats confirmed HIV and should not be casually interrupted.
PrEP: is ongoing HIV prevention for people without HIV; confirm HIV status and use current baseline/follow-up guidance.
PEP: is time sensitive after a potential exposure; evaluate rapidly when care is sought within 72 hours.
Interactions: antacids/mineral products, acid suppression, and many common drugs can matter—check the exact regimen.
STI care: includes site-specific testing, treatment, partner services, prevention, and retesting as indicated.
Pregnancy and assault: require prompt, coordinated, trauma-informed care.
FNP standard: combine current guideline use with confidentiality, respect, medication safety, and rapid linkage to appropriate care.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. HIV testing, ART, PrEP, PEP, STI testing/treatment, pregnancy care, partner services, reporting, medication selection, interaction management, and follow-up must follow current CDC/NIH guidance, product labeling, local law and policy, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
